chapter: New Orleans, Havana and back to New York
title: Huey Long at the Roosevelt Hotel in New Orleans
summary: The band was the first out-of-town band in the Roosevelt's Fountain Room; Huey Long dined there nightly and requested songs, and Barnet denies he complained of volume.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Well, the Roosevelt Hotel came after, directly after, the Park Central. I remember we were there New Years Eve of '34 going into '35. And we were the first out of town band to play the room, and it was -- we used to play the dinner session in the Fountain Room, and Huey Long used to be in there every night for dinner. And he had these bodyguards around him, and they would sit, facing the backs of the chairs, looking around the rest of the room, and Huey would stuff his napkin in his neck and eat up a storm and send requests over to the band. He liked, 'Stars Fell on Alabama.' I don't know why, but that and that Jack Benny theme song, 'Love in Bloom.' And then we played the dinner session there, and then we'd have to pack the instruments up and go into the Blue Room, and we'd go through the lobby. And of course this was the first out of town band, and as we'd go through the lobby you could hear mutterings like, 'Damn yankees.' We weren't very popular there. At the time.
Some book says that Huey Long complained that the band was too loud and that the management told you to play softer and you wouldn't.
Oh, that's a lot of baloney. Huey never complained about anything. In fact he was a doll. In fact I was even his guest in the Unites States Senate later on.
Oh. I'm just trying to remember which --
I don't know where some of these things get started, but --
I think it was -- let's see.
The guy that did the complaining about being too loud was Seymour Weiss, the owner of the hotel.
